title: Germany and Austria
lead: Cool vineyards on rivers. Germany grades wine by grape ripeness and is famous for Riesling. Austria is known for dry Grüner Veltliner from the Danube.

intro.title: THE GERMAN LADDER
intro.text: German wine law has four tiers. The top two must come 100% from one of the 13 regions.

tiers.name: Prädikatswein
tiers.note: Graded by grape ripeness. No added sugar.

sections.name: Germany: cool climate, river slopes

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Cool continental. Vineyards sit at 49°N and above, mostly in the southwest of the country.

lines.label: Rivers
lines.text: The Rhine and its tributaries soften the climate. The water reflects sunlight back onto steep, south-facing slopes.

know: Riesling is Germany's most planted and most important grape.
Spätburgunder is the German name for Pinot Noir.
Winemakers often leave sugar in the wine to balance high acidity, so off-dry wines are low in alcohol.
Chaptalization means adding sugar to the juice before fermentation to raise the alcohol.
Germany has 13 wine regions, called Anbaugebiete.

visuals.title: Anbaugebiete
visuals.text: Germany's official wine regions. Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein must come 100% from one of them.

sections.name: The Prädikat ladder

lines.label: How it works
lines.text: Prädikatswein is graded by how ripe the grapes were at harvest. No sugar may be added.

lines.label: Watch out
lines.text: Ripeness is not sweetness. The winemaker decides how sweet the finished wine is, so Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese can all be made trocken (dry).

know: The order, least to most ripe: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Trockenbeerenauslese.
Eiswein grapes must be frozen, picked at minus 7°C or colder, with no noble rot.
Eiswein has the same ripeness level as Beerenauslese.
Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are very sweet and usually made from noble-rot (botrytis) grapes.
Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) is the top of the pyramid and can't be made every year.

visuals.title: Six Prädikate, least to most ripe

rows.name: Kabinett
rows.meta: Light, low alcohol. Off-dry or trocken

rows.name: Auslese
rows.meta: Fully ripe grapes, unripe ones sorted out. Often off-dry

rows.name: Eiswein
rows.meta: Frozen grapes. Same ripeness as BA

visuals.note: Ripeness is measured in degrees Oechsle (°Oe). The minimums change by region and grape.

sections.name: Dry or sweet? Label words

lines.label: On the label
lines.text: Trocken means dry. Halbtrocken means half-dry. Feinherb is an unofficial word for off-dry.

lines.label: The rule
lines.text: A dry German wine has up to 4 g of sugar per liter, or up to 9 g if the wine is acidic enough.

know: Trocken = dry.
Halbtrocken = half-dry (semi-dry), up to 12 g/l, or 18 g/l with enough acidity.
Feinherb is not defined by wine law and usually sits between semi-dry and sweet.
Edelfäule is the German word for noble rot.

visuals.title: German sweetness · sugar per liter
visuals.note: Top limits shown. Dry is up to 4 g, or 9 g with high acidity. Feinherb has no legal limit.

sections.name: VDP and the vineyard pyramid

lines.label: Who
lines.text: The VDP is a private association of top estates. It ranks vineyards on the Burgundy model.

lines.label: Level
lines.text: The Court puts the VDP in the Certified column. Know the name and the top terms.

know: Grosses Gewächs (GG) is a dry wine from a VDP.Grosse Lage, the top vineyard level.
Erstes Gewächs is the single-vineyard premier cru level.
VDP wines carry an eagle on the bottle neck.
German law now ranks wines by how small the place is: region, village, single vineyard.

rows.name: VDP.Grosse Lage
rows.note: Grand cru sites. Dry wines are Grosses Gewächs

sections.name: Mosel

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Steep slate slopes along the Mosel River and its small tributaries, the Saar and Ruwer.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Riesling, light in alcohol, from dry to noble-sweet.

know: Mosel soil is slate. It is porous and holds heat.
South-facing slopes catch the sun. Half the vineyards are steeper than 30 degrees.
Villages to know: Erden, Ürzig, Wehlen, Bernkastel-Kues, Piesport.
The Mosel is considered Germany's oldest wine region.

sections.name: Rheingau, Rheinhessen, Pfalz

lines.label: Setting
lines.text: Three regions on the Rhine. Each makes Riesling. Rheingau and Pfalz also grow Spätburgunder.

know: Rheingau is one long south-facing slope above the Rhine, sheltered by mountains to the north.
Johannisberg is the Rheingau village to recognize. It is where Spätlese was born, in 1775.
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest region in size and production.
Pfalz is a continuation of Alsace. It is one of Germany's warmest areas and focuses on dry wines.

items.label: RHEINGAU
items.title: Riesling on the Rhine
items.text:
South-facing slope on the Rhine
Highest share of Riesling in Germany
Village: Johannisberg

items.label: PFALZ
items.title: Warm, dry wines
items.text:
Continuation of Alsace
One of Germany's warmest areas
Germany's largest red wine region

visuals.title: Rheinhessen
visuals.text: Germany's largest wine region by size and production.

sections.name: Austria

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Eastern Austria, continental climate, foothills of the Alps along the Danube River.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Unlike Germany, Austria makes very dry or very sweet whites, with no off-dry styles today. New oak is rare for whites.

know: Grüner Veltliner is Austria's best-known grape, a native white.
Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch are the red grapes to know.
DAC is Austria's appellation system, like AOC or DOC, focused on dry wines.
Prädikatswein exists in Austria but is rarely made.
Austrian Qualitätswein carries a capsule on the bottle, called the Banderole.

visuals.title: Austrian wine law, top to bottom

rows.name: DAC
rows.note: Appellation of origin. Set grapes and styles

sections.name: Wachau, Kremstal, Kamptal

lines.label: Place
lines.text: Three DACs in Niederösterreich (Lower Austria). The Wachau is the Danube valley between Melk and Krems.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Dry whites from Grüner Veltliner and Riesling, on steep terraces above the river.

know: The Wachau has its own system based on grape ripeness: Steinfeder, Federspiel, Smaragd.
Smaragd is the ripest and most powerful level, named for green lizards in the vineyards.
All three Wachau styles are dry, with no oak taste.
Kremstal and Kamptal sit on Danube tributaries and make dry Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.

items.name: Steinfeder
items.text: Light and fragrant. Named for feather grass

items.name: Smaragd
items.text: Powerful, ageworthy. Named for the emerald lizard

mixups.why: Same ripeness. Eiswein grapes are frozen with no noble rot; BA is usually botrytis.
Trocken on a label means dry. TBA is a very sweet wine from shriveled noble-rot berries.
Halbtrocken has legal sugar limits. Feinherb is an unofficial term for off-dry.
Both are Wachau styles. Smaragd is the ripest (12.5%+); Steinfeder is the lightest (up to 11.5%).

sources: Court of Master Sommeliers Americas Introductory Course Guide and Curriculum Guide; German Wine Institute (winesofgermany.com, where germanwines.de now redirects); VDP; Vinea Wachau; Weinviertel DAC; Wine Folly as a labelled secondary source. Checked Oct 31, 2026.

facts.fact: Court Course Guide Section 6 covers Germany (Mosel, Rheingau, Rheinhessen, Pfalz) and Austria (Niederösterreich, Kremstal, Kamptal, Wachau).

Intro learning outcome (Germany): understand climate, the importance of rivers, soil types, grapes and selected regions; recognize the hierarchy Wein, Qualitätswein, Prädikatswein and the progression of Prädikat levels.
Germany: northerly location, vineyards planted at 49°N and above; most wine regions are in the southwest corner of the country. Climate: cool continental.

Germany: the Rhine and its tributaries moderate the climate; rivers reflect sunlight back up to the vineyards, adding warmth for ripening. Mountains protect from cold north winds and create rain shadows.
Germany grape growing: steep, south-facing hillsides maximize sun exposure and warmth; cool growing seasons.

German winemaking: large wooden fuder or stück casks or stainless steel; residual sugar often left to counterbalance acidity; alcohol in off-dry wine is generally low; wines can be dry, off-dry or lusciously sweet.
Chaptalization: adding sugar to unfermented grape must to increase alcohol after fermentation; used when grapes do not reach enough sugar ripeness.

German grapes (Intro): Riesling, the most planted and most important; red Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir). Certified column adds Müller-Thurgau, Silvaner, Weissburgunder (Pinot Blanc), Grauburgunder (Pinot Gris).
German law (Intro): Deutscher Wein (no geographic indication); Landwein (regional); Qualitätswein (quality wine from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete); Prädikatswein (prädikat means 'distinction').
Prädikatswein: a subset of Qualitätswein graded by ripeness (sugar in the grapes) at harvest; considered the highest quality level for wines with residual sugar; chaptalization is not allowed.

Six Prädikate in order of ripeness: 1 Kabinett (off-dry, can be trocken); 2 Spätlese (off-dry, can be trocken); 3 Auslese (often off-dry, sometimes trocken); 4 Beerenauslese (very sweet, often botrytis); 5 Eiswein (very sweet, grapes frozen, no botrytis, same ripeness as Beerenauslese); 6 Trockenbeerenauslese (very sweet).
Prädikat levels are set by ripeness at harvest, but choices in the winery decide the finished sweetness.

Kabinett: fine, light wines from ripe grapes with low alcohol. Spätlese: harvested a little later, more intense, not necessarily sweet. Auslese: fully ripe grapes, unripe berries separated out, not always sweet.
Beerenauslese: individually selected overripe berries usually infected by Botrytis cinerea (noble rot); can be stored for decades.
Ice wine: grapes as ripe as BA, harvested at minus 7°C or colder and pressed frozen; becoming rarer as winters get warmer.
Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) is the top of the quality pyramid: shrunken, shriveled noble-rot berries that cannot be harvested every vintage; can age for decades.
Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein must come 100% from one of the 13 German growing regions and pass the quality wine test; Qualitätswein may be chaptalized, Prädikat wines may not.
Must weight is measured in degrees Oechsle (°Oe), named after Ferdinand Oechsle. Minimum must weight for Auslese is 83 to 100 °Oe and for ice wine 110 to 128 °Oe, depending on region.

Label terms: Trocken = dry (Intro column). Halbtrocken = half-dry; Edelfäule = noble rot; Schloss = castle (Certified column). Anbaugebiete = one of 13 growing regions; Prädikate = quality levels based on ripeness (Intro).

German sweetness: dry = up to 4 g/l residual sugar, or up to 9 g/l if total acidity is no more than 2 g/l lower than the sugar. Semi-dry = up to 12 g/l, or up to 18 g/l if sugar exceeds acidity by no more than 10 g. Semi-sweet = up to 45 g/l. Sweet = from 45 g/l.
Feinherb is an unofficial term, not regulated by wine law, usually placed between semi-dry and sweet. Half of German Qualität and Prädikat wines were marketed dry in 2022.

VDP (Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter) is in the Court's Certified column: a national association of producers with its own classification on the Burgundy model. Grosses Gewächs = single-vineyard grand cru wines; Erstes Gewächs = single-vineyard premier cru wines.

VDP classification has four levels: VDP.Grosse Lage, VDP.Erste Lage, VDP.Ortswein, VDP.Gutswein. Dry wines from Grosse Lage vineyards are called VDP.Grosses Gewächs. It is the VDP's private rule, not German wine law. All VDP wines carry the VDP eagle on the bottleneck. Four-tier model adopted 2012.

German wine law amended 2021: origin becomes decisive for quality ('the more precisely defined the origin, the higher the quality'); new rules binding from the 2026 vintage; Prädikat levels Kabinett to TBA remain unaffected.

New PDO origin pyramid has four levels: wine-growing region; Region wines (defined areas or former Grosslagen); village wines (Ortsweine); single-vineyard wines, topped by Grosses Gewächs then Erstes Gewächs. Grosses Gewächs must be trocken.
Mosel (Intro): along the Mosel River; porous, heat-retaining slate; south-facing vineyards; Riesling. Recognize villages Erden, Ürzig, Wehlen, Bernkastel-Kues, Piesport.

Mosel: with its tributaries Saar and Ruwer it forms one region, considered the oldest in Germany; half of vineyards are on slopes over 30 degrees; 5,156 ha of Riesling; Europe's steepest vineyard, the Bremmer Calmont, is here.
Pfalz (Intro): continuation of Alsace, mountain protection, Rhine moderates climate; one of the warmest areas in Germany; focus on dry wines; Riesling and Spätburgunder.
Pfalz is Germany's second-largest region (23,640 ha); Riesling is number one there; it is Germany's largest red wine region.
Rheinhessen (Intro): the largest Anbaugebiet in size and production volume; Rhine River; Riesling.
Rheinhessen: 27,657 ha; Germany's largest wine-growing region.

Rheingau (Intro): mountains protect from the cold north; a long south-facing slope facing the Rhine, which moderates and reflects light; continental; Riesling and Spätburgunder; recognize Johannisberg.

Rheingau has the highest percentage of Riesling of any German region. In 1775 the monks of Kloster Johannisberg discovered the advantages of a late harvest; Johannisberg is the birthplace of Spätlese.
Germany has 13 growing areas.
Germany is the world leader in Riesling and Pinot Blanc cultivation.
Certified column: the 1971 German Wine Law made ripeness at harvest the prime determinant of quality.
Sweet wines (Intro): German noble-rot wines are Auslese, Beerenauslese and TBA; Eiswein is made in Germany and Austria.
Intro learning outcome (Austria): identify and locate major regions and appellations, geographic features, major grapes, and how Austrian wines differ from German wines.
Austria: Eastern Austria; continental climate; foothills of the Alps; Danube River; steep hillsides overlooking the Danube and its tributaries.
Austrian winemaking: very dry or very sweet white wine, no current production of off-dry styles; new oak is rarely used for white wine.
Austrian grapes (Intro): white Grüner Veltliner; red Zweigelt and Blaufränkisch. Riesling sits in the Certified column.

Austrian law (Intro): Wein; Landwein (regional, rarely exported); Qualitätswein; DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus), an appellation of origin like AOC or DOC with set grapes and styles, focused on dry wines; Prädikatswein like Germany but rarely produced.
Wachau has its own classification based on grape ripeness at harvest; Smaragd is the highest ripeness, named for green lizards (Intro). Steinfeder and Federspiel are in the Certified column.

Austria (Intro): region Niederösterreich (Lower Austria) with sub-regions Kamptal DAC, Kremstal DAC, Wachau DAC; recognize an Austrian wine capsule. Certified: Kremstal and Kamptal make dry whites from Grüner Veltliner and Riesling; the capsule is the Banderole.
Certified column pairing: Grüner Veltliner is unoaked, crisp and dry; good with fresh seafood, smoked fish, vegetables and herbs, and hard-to-pair asparagus and artichokes.

Vinea Wachau styles: all white, dry, no oak. Steinfeder up to 11.5% alcohol, named for feather grass. Federspiel not more than 12.5%, named for falconry bait. Smaragd at least 12.5%, named for the emerald-green lizard. Registered trademarks for member wineries only.
Wachau DAC: Gebietswein, Ortswein, Riedenwein; 100% hand-harvested grapes; Riedenwein only Grüner Veltliner or Riesling.
Wachau: the Danube valley between Melk and Krems, 33 km of river; terraces up to about 450 m; weathered primary rock soils (gneiss) with loess lower down.
Weinviertel has about 6,200 ha of Grüner Veltliner, half of Austria's plantings; Weinviertel DAC means peppery Grüner Veltliner.

Wine Folly (secondary): Grüner Veltliner is Austria's native star grape; Niederösterreich is Austria's largest wine region; Wachau, Kremstal and Kamptal produce its highest-rated wines; Zweigelt, the most planted red, is a cross of St. Laurent and Blaufränkisch; after a 1985 scandal Austria tightened regulation.
Wine Folly (secondary): Vinea Wachau Nobilis Districtus was founded in 1983; it is not part of Austrian wine law and plays a role similar to Germany's VDP.

unverified: austrianwine.com (Austrian Wine) blocks automated access with a bot check, so nothing from it could be fetched. Austrian facts come from the Court, Vinea Wachau, Weinviertel DAC and Wine Folly (secondary).
The current number and full list of Austrian DACs was not confirmed. Wine Folly's figure ('10 of the 16 wine regions') looks out of date and was not used.

Minimum Oechsle for each Prädikat was not confirmed from an official page (DWI gives ranges only for Auslese, 83-100 °Oe, and Eiswein, 110-128 °Oe). Wine Folly's ranges differ from DWI (for example Auslese 83-110) and were not used.
germanwines.de now redirects to winesofgermany.com (the German Wine Institute's international site); all DWI facts cite winesofgermany.com.
The Court's Germany location line names borders with 'France, Belgium and Switzerland'; this was not repeated because it could not be checked against DWI.
Bar lengths in the sweetness scale are drawn from the legal maximums (9, 18, 45 g/l) for display only.

Court column split (Introductory vs Certified) was read from the PDF's text positions; VDP, Halbtrocken, Steinfeder, Federspiel, Austrian Riesling and the Banderole sit in the Certified column and are included as context.
